meta.blurb: Bathsheba Everdene turns down the shepherd who loves her, then inherits a farm and runs it alone. One careless joke, a valentine sent for fun, brings a rich farmer to her door. A soldier with a sword is waiting in the woods.
meta.bible:
Gabriel Oak: a young sheep farmer, honest, patient, loyal; plays the flute; later Bathsheba's shepherd and bailiff. Bathsheba Everdene: a beautiful, proud, independent young woman who inherits her uncle's farm at Weatherbury. William Boldwood: a rich, serious, middle-aged farmer, about forty, a bachelor. Sergeant Frank Troy: a handsome, careless soldier. Fanny Robin: a young servant girl on Bathsheba's farm who loves Troy. Liddy Smallbury: Bathsheba's young maid and companion. Joseph Poorgrass: a shy, timid farm worker. Jan Coggan: a wise, good-humoured farm worker. Pennyways: the dishonest bailiff whom Bathsheba dismisses. Norcombe Hill: where Gabriel keeps sheep. Weatherbury: the village and Bathsheba's farm. Casterbridge: the market town; its hiring fair, corn market and workhouse. Bath: the city where Bathsheba and Troy marry in secret. Lulworth Cove: the bay on the Dorset coast where Troy swims. Dorset. California: where Gabriel thinks of going. Malthouse: the old building where workers drink and talk. Valentine. Christmas. Voice and tone: warm, wise and rural, with gentle humour; deaths are stated plainly, with no gore; Boldwood shoots Troy at his Christmas party and is sentenced to death, then reprieved; set in the English countryside of the 1800s. Mark Clark: a farm worker and drinking companion. Henery Fray: a farm worker who resents losing the bailiff's post. Cainy Ball: a young farm lad. Teddy Coggan: a small boy of the village.
All Saints and All Souls: the two churches in Casterbridge; Fanny waited at All Saints, Troy at All Souls.
Gabriel is twenty-eight when the story begins. Fanny and her baby die in the Casterbridge workhouse and are buried at Weatherbury; Gabriel rubs out the words and child from the coffin lid. Troy buys a headstone and plants flowers that the rain from the church gargoyle washes away. Boldwood's promise: Bathsheba will marry him after six years if Troy is not found. Boldwood's Christmas party is on Christmas Eve. Boldwood is tried at the Casterbridge assizes, sentenced to death, then spared and sent to prison. Gabriel becomes Bathsheba's bailiff after Troy's drowning and plans to go to California before they marry in spring.

beats.summary: Boldwood asks again for her answer.

B1B2: Gabriel Oak is a young farmer who keeps a small flock on Norcombe Hill. He works hard every day and hopes that one day he will own a bigger farm.
In the evening Gabriel sits outside his little hut and plays the flute. His old dog lies beside him, while the young one watches the sheep.
One cold morning Gabriel sees a wagon moving slowly along the road below the hill. It is loaded with tables, chairs and boxes, and a pretty girl sits on top.
Thinking that nobody can see her, the girl takes out a small mirror. She smiles at her own face, and Gabriel smiles at her.
At the toll gate the keeper asks for his fee, but the girl has no coin to give him. Gabriel steps forward and quietly pays the two pence himself.
The girl does not say thank you, and the wagon rolls away with her chin held high. Gabriel is amused by her pride, but he is also a little hurt.
A few days later a neighbour tells Gabriel the girl's name. She is Bathsheba Everdene, and she has come to live with her aunt at a farm nearby.
Gabriel chooses a small lamb that has lost its mother, and he wraps it in his coat. Then he carries it across the wet fields to the aunt's farm as a gift.
Bathsheba takes the lamb and thanks him politely, although her eyes are laughing at his clumsy words. Her aunt asks him to visit again, and Gabriel goes away very happy.
That night Gabriel walks back up the hill under a clear, cold sky. He is sure that he has found the woman he wants to marry.
For weeks Gabriel cannot get Bathsheba out of his mind, even while he counts the sheep. He makes mistakes that he has never made before, and his old dog looks at him in surprise.
At last Gabriel decides that he must ask Bathsheba to be his wife. He brushes his best coat, combs his hair, and sets off down the hill with a beating heart.
The fields are wet and the road is muddy, but Gabriel hardly notices. At the farm he finds Bathsheba alone beside a gate, with the evening light behind her.
Gabriel tells her plainly that he loves her and wants her to be his wife. He promises her a good home, a piano of her own, and all the care that a man can give.
Bathsheba listens to the end, and then she shakes her head with a small smile. She says that she does not love him and that she wants a husband who could tame her.
Gabriel says that he will love her all his life and that she will never be lonely. But Bathsheba steps back and says that she hates the idea of belonging to anyone.
Gabriel begs her not to be angry, but she turns and walks away along the lane. He stands beside the gate with his hat in his hands and watches her until she is gone.
A few days later Gabriel hears that Bathsheba has left the district. Nobody can tell him where she has gone, and after a while he stops asking.
Gabriel goes back to his flock and tells himself that he must work hard and forget. It is good advice, but it is much easier to give than to follow.
When lambing time comes, the hill is full of new lambs, and Gabriel hardly sleeps for a week. The neighbours begin to say that the young shepherd is careful, honest and cleverer than his years.
Gabriel's old dog is calm and clever, and it knows every part of the work. The young dog is full of energy, but nobody has taught it to be careful.
After many nights without sleep, Gabriel is so tired that he cannot keep his eyes open. He lies down in his hut and leaves the flock to the dogs.
Outside, the moon is bright, and for a while the sheep lie quietly on the grass. Then the young dog jumps up and begins to chase them, only for the fun of it.
The frightened sheep run across the dark hill, and the young dog follows close behind. The old dog barks a warning, but the sheep cannot see where the ground ends.
The sheep in front reach the old chalk pit and cannot stop. One after another they go over the edge and fall into the darkness.
Gabriel wakes at dawn and steps out of his hut into the cold light. The field is empty, and he follows the marks of the hooves across the hill.
Gabriel reaches the edge of the chalk pit and looks down. His whole flock lies dead at the bottom, and there is nothing he can do.
Gabriel finds the young dog sitting in the grass, ashamed and confused. It meant no harm, but it can never be trusted with sheep again, and it has to be put down.
Gabriel had borrowed money to buy his sheep, and he had no insurance. Now he must sell nearly everything he owns to pay what he owes.
When the last bill is paid, Gabriel has almost nothing left. He owns his crook, his flute, a few clothes and a handful of coins.
Early one morning Gabriel leaves Norcombe Hill for the last time. He carries a bag, his crook and his flute, and he is looking for work.
On fair day the market square in Casterbridge is full of men who want work. Each man carries the sign of his trade, and shepherds hold their crooks.
Gabriel stands in a row of shepherds from the morning until the evening. Farmers look at him and walk past, because there are too many men and too few places.
When the crowd goes home, Gabriel is still without work. He decides to try another town, and he sets off along the dark road.
Tired out, Gabriel climbs into a wagon full of hay and falls asleep. When he wakes in the night, he sees a red glow in the sky far ahead of him.
He arrives at a farm where the great stacks of hay are on fire. The workers are running in every direction, but nobody knows what to do.
Gabriel sees at once that someone must give orders, and so he does. He tells the men to fetch water and wet sacks and to pull the burning straw away from the stacks.
Gabriel climbs to the top of the largest stack, where the heat is fiercest. There he beats out the sparks with a wet sack while the men below pass him water.
At last the fire is out, and the rest of the hay is safe. The black-faced men sit on the ground, and they look at the stranger with new respect.
As the sun rises, a young woman in a long shawl walks across the yard. She is the owner of the farm, and she has come to find out who saved it.
As she comes closer, Gabriel knows her face at once. It is Bathsheba Everdene, the proud girl who once refused to marry him.
Bathsheba thanks him warmly and asks if there is anything that he needs. Gabriel says that he is a shepherd and that he is looking for a place.
Bathsheba says that she badly needs a good shepherd, and that she will hire him now. Gabriel agrees at once, and he is glad to have work and a roof.
A young maid called Liddy Smallbury brings Gabriel bread, cheese and milk. She talks all the time, and in ten minutes he knows all the news of the farm.
The next morning Bathsheba gathers all her workers in the yard. She tells them that she will not hire a bailiff, because she will manage the farm herself.
Bathsheba then turns to Pennyways, the old bailiff of the farm. She tells him that she knows he has been stealing from the farm and that he must leave at once.
The workers watch Pennyways walk away down the road. Some of them are impressed by their young mistress, but others doubt that a woman can run a farm.
From that day Bathsheba rises early and walks round her fields and barns. In the evening she sits over her account books until the candle burns low.
In the evenings the workers gather in the old malthouse, where a warm fire glows. Jan Coggan, Joseph Poorgrass, Mark Clark, Henery Fray and young Cainy Ball are always there.
Gabriel walks into the malthouse, and the men turn to look at the stranger. He sits down quietly, says very little, and little by little they begin to trust him.
One evening the men talk about Fanny Robin, a young servant girl who has vanished from the farm. Nobody knows where she went, but some say that a soldier is the reason.
Henery Fray complains that he should have been made bailiff. Old Jan Coggan only laughs, and says that the new mistress has more sense than every man in the room.
It is late when Gabriel leaves the malthouse and sets off for home. The road is dark, the wind is cold, and nobody else is about.
A pale young woman steps out of the shadows and begs him to stop. Gabriel sees by the faint light that she is Fanny Robin, the girl who left the farm.
Fanny says that she is going to marry a soldier, but she has no money for the journey. She begs Gabriel to help her, and to tell nobody that he has seen her.
Gabriel puts every coin that he has into her hand. She thanks him, wipes her eyes, and hurries away along the road toward Casterbridge.
Fanny's soldier is Sergeant Troy, who is stationed in Casterbridge. He is handsome and charming, and he has promised to marry her.
On the morning of the wedding Fanny puts on her best dress and hurries to the church. Her heart is beating fast, and she is afraid of being late.
But Fanny has gone to All Saints, and Troy is waiting at All Souls across the town. Nobody comes to marry him, and the clock moves slowly on.
Troy is angry and ashamed, and he will not forgive her mistake. Fanny, in tears, is left alone in the street.
On market day Bathsheba drives into Casterbridge to sell her corn. She is the only woman among the farmers, and she walks in with her head high.
Every man in the market turns to look at her as she passes. Bathsheba pretends not to notice, but she is secretly pleased.
Only one man in the market does not look at her. He is Farmer Boldwood, a serious and wealthy man who stands apart with his back turned.
On the way home Bathsheba asks Liddy about the man who did not look. Liddy says that Boldwood is rich and unmarried, and that he has never loved any woman.
On Valentine's Day, Bathsheba and Liddy find a pretty card with a verse on it. Liddy says that they should send it to someone, just for fun.
Liddy suggests little Teddy Coggan, but Bathsheba would like a bigger joke. She says they will toss a hymn-book to decide: if it falls open, the card will go to Boldwood.
Bathsheba tosses the hymn-book into the air, and it falls open on the floor. The two girls look at each other, and then they laugh and laugh.
Bathsheba takes a stick of red sealing wax and warms it over a candle. She presses it onto the card, and the seal bears the words Marry me.
Liddy laughs so much that she can hardly stand up. Bathsheba writes Boldwood's name on the card, and a boy takes it to his house that evening.
At breakfast the next day Boldwood finds a strange card beside his plate. He breaks the red seal and slowly reads the words Marry me.
Boldwood puts the card on the shelf above his fire. All day he finds himself looking at it, and he cannot think about his work.
On Sunday in church, Boldwood looks at Bathsheba for the first time in his life. She keeps her eyes on her book, but a blush rises in her cheeks.
Boldwood cannot sleep, and he walks up and down his house at night. He had thought that his heart was a quiet lake, but now a storm has come.
At last Boldwood puts on his best coat and rides to Bathsheba's farm. His manner is calm and composed, although his heart is beating much faster than usual.
Boldwood speaks to Bathsheba at her door in a quiet, serious voice. He tells her that he loves her, and he asks her to be his wife.
Bathsheba is shocked, and she says that she does not love him. But she cannot bring herself to refuse him at once, so she promises to think about it.
When Boldwood has gone, Bathsheba sits alone and feels ashamed. Her joke was only for fun, but now a good man's heart is part of it.
The men in the malthouse are all talking about Boldwood's visit to the farm. Gabriel listens, and he thinks that Bathsheba has done a cruel thing.
Gabriel finds Bathsheba in the farmyard and tells her plainly what he thinks. He says that her valentine was a cruel joke, and that Boldwood is not a man to play with.
Bathsheba's face goes red with anger, and she tells Gabriel that he has no right to speak to her so. She says that he may leave her farm at once.
Gabriel packs his bag and says goodbye to the workers in the yard. Nobody wants him to go, but he walks out of the gate without looking back.
A few days later the sheep find a gap in the fence and rush into a field of clover. They eat as much as they can, because it is fresh and sweet.
Too much clover is dangerous for sheep, because it fills them with gas. Soon many of the animals are lying on the ground, and some are already dying.
Bathsheba runs out to the field as fast as she can. She sees her sheep lying on the grass and the workers standing helplessly around them.
A boy runs across the fields to find Gabriel and tells him the news. Gabriel says that he will not return unless the mistress asks him herself.
When she hears this, Bathsheba forgets her pride and goes to find him. With her voice shaking, she begs him to come back and save her sheep.
Gabriel takes a small, hollow, pointed tool from his pocket. He kneels beside the nearest sheep and makes one careful hole in its side.
The sheep takes a deep breath, gets up and begins to walk, and the men cheer. Gabriel goes on from one animal to the next until every sick one has been treated.
At the end of the night Bathsheba thanks Gabriel with tears in her eyes. She tells him that she cannot manage without him, and she asks him to stay.
Gabriel says that he will stay, and he is glad to be back. The men tell the story of that night in the malthouse for months afterwards.
In early summer the workers wash the sheep in a deep pool by the river. Bathsheba stands on the bank and watches, and the sun shines on the water.
Boldwood rides up to the pool, saying that he has come on business, but he never looks at the sheep. He stands on the bank and watches Bathsheba, and he does not look away.
Gabriel sees the look in Boldwood's eyes, and he understands it very well. He says nothing, because it is not his place, but it makes him sad.
A few days later the shearing begins in the great barn. Gabriel is the quickest shearer of all, and the wool piles up beside him.
When the last sheep is done, there is a big supper in the barn. The tables are full of meat, bread and cider, and the lanterns glow overhead.
Boldwood arrives late, and Bathsheba asks him to sit beside her. She is polite, but she is nervous, because she knows why he has come.
When the singing is loud, Boldwood leans toward her and speaks quietly. He asks her for her answer, and he tells her that he cannot wait for ever.
Bathsheba does not want to answer him in a room full of people. She tells him gently that he will have his answer before long.
A few evenings later Bathsheba walks round her fields alone in the dark. She likes to see that everything is safe before she goes to bed.
On the way home she goes through a thick wood of fir trees. It is very dark, and she walks carefully along the narrow path.
In the dark wood Bathsheba walks into a man coming the other way. Her dress catches on something sharp, and she cannot move.
The sharp thing is the spur on a soldier's boot. The man is very polite, but he does not seem to be in a hurry to free her.
The soldier opens a small lantern, and its light falls on his face. He is young and very handsome, and his coat is a brilliant scarlet.
The soldier tells her that his name is Sergeant Troy. He says that she is the most beautiful woman he has ever seen, and he does not seem to be joking.
At last Troy frees her dress, and Bathsheba hurries away along the path. She tells herself that she is angry with him, but she is smiling in the dark.
The next day, to Bathsheba's surprise, Troy walks into her hayfield. He takes a rake from one of the men and works beside her all afternoon.
Troy asks Bathsheba whether she has ever seen the sword exercise. When she says no, he promises to show her in a quiet place at sundown.
At sundown Bathsheba goes to a hollow that is full of tall green ferns. Troy is waiting there, and his sword shines in the last of the light.
Troy tells her to stand still, and then he begins to swing his sword. It flashes round her in bright circles, close to her head, but it never touches her.
With one last stroke Troy cuts off a curl of her hair and holds it on the point of his sword. Bathsheba is frightened and dazzled at the same time.
Bathsheba cannot stop thinking about the soldier, and she hardly eats her dinner. Liddy sees at once that her mistress is in love.
Soon the men in the malthouse are talking about the soldier and their mistress. Gabriel hears it all, and he knows that he must speak.
Gabriel finds Bathsheba in the farmyard and speaks gravely. He tells her that Sergeant Troy is not a good man, and that he will make her unhappy.
Bathsheba is very angry, and she says that it is not his business. She tells him that he may leave, but Gabriel says nothing and stays.
Boldwood hears the same story from his own servants. He cannot believe that Bathsheba could prefer a careless soldier to him.
One dark night Boldwood meets Troy on the road to Casterbridge, and he steps out of the shadows. He seizes the soldier's arm and holds it in a tight and trembling grip.
Boldwood forgets his pride and begs Troy to leave Bathsheba alone. He says that he loves her deeply, and that a soldier can only bring her sorrow.
But Troy only laughs at him, in a light and careless way that hurts. He says that he will do as he likes, and that Boldwood should go home and be sensible.
A few days later Troy goes away to the city of Bath. He says goodbye to nobody, and he leaves no message for Bathsheba.
Bathsheba hears that Troy has gone away, and she cannot rest. Her pride tells her to forget him, but her heart tells her to follow.
After a long journey Bathsheba reaches Bath, a big city full of strangers. She has never been there before, and she does not know where to look for Troy.
At last she sees Troy walking in the street, and he stares at her in surprise. Then he smiles his charming smile and takes both her hands.
Troy tells her that he has thought of nothing but her since he left. He says that they should marry at once, before anyone can stop them.
Bathsheba knows that she is being foolish, but she cannot say no. She has always done as she liked, and now she says yes.
They are married quietly in a church in Bath, with no friends and no family. Nobody at Weatherbury knows anything about the wedding at all.
A few days later they travel back to Weatherbury together. Bathsheba is proud and happy, but she is afraid of what the village will say.
That evening Bathsheba calls all the workers into the yard. She stands beside her husband and tells them that she is now Mrs Troy.
The workers are astonished and say very little in the yard. Afterwards, in the malthouse, they shake their heads and wonder how long such a marriage can last.
Gabriel hears the news in silence and goes on with his work. He warned her, and he was right, but he takes no pleasure in it.
Boldwood hears the news the next day, and it is a terrible blow. He shuts himself in his big house and speaks to nobody.
Troy soon takes charge of the farm and begins to give orders to the men. He knows nothing about farming, and the workers do not respect him.
Troy goes to the horse races at Casterbridge and bets Bathsheba's money on the horses. He believes that he cannot lose, but he loses a great deal.
Bathsheba looks at her account books and sees that the money is going fast. She says nothing, but at night she lies awake and worries.
The harvest is ready, but the stacks have not yet been covered. Troy ignores the work and plans a big supper for the men.
At the supper Troy pours drink for everyone, and the men grow noisy and then sleepy. One after another they fall asleep on the floor, but Gabriel stays sober.
Outside, Gabriel sees many signs that a great storm is coming. A toad crawls over the path, slugs are creeping toward the house, and the sheep stand huddled together.
Gabriel goes back and tries to wake the men, but nobody will move. He decides to cover the stacks himself, and Bathsheba comes out to help.
The first thunder rolls across the sky, and a great wind rises. Gabriel and Bathsheba pull the heavy covers over the highest stacks.
Lightning flashes all around them, and the rain begins to fall. Bathsheba holds the ladder while Gabriel climbs up to tie the covers down.
By morning the storm has passed, and the harvest is saved. Bathsheba thanks Gabriel, and then she looks at her husband, who is still asleep in the barn.
Fanny is weak and ill, and she has nowhere to go. She decides to walk to the workhouse in Casterbridge, where poor people can find a bed.
She walks along the lonely road for many miles. She rests at every milestone, but she grows weaker with every step.
A large dog comes out of the dusk and walks beside her. It seems to understand that she is in trouble, and it will not leave her.
At last Fanny reaches the gate of the workhouse, and the people inside take her in. She is too weak to say more than a few words.
Fanny dies in the workhouse before morning, and her newborn baby dies too. Nobody at Weatherbury knows yet what has happened to her.
The news reaches Weatherbury, and it is decided that Fanny will be buried in the village where she lived. A farm cart is sent to Casterbridge to bring her home.
Joseph Poorgrass is a shy and nervous man, and he does not like his sad task. He loads the coffin onto the cart and starts on the long road home.
On the road Joseph passes an inn, and his courage fails. He tells himself that one drink will calm his nerves, and he goes inside.
Inside, he finds some old friends, who are glad to see him and want all the news. One drink becomes two, then three, and the hours slowly go by.
At last Joseph remembers the coffin and hurries out to the cart. He drives on toward Weatherbury, and it is very late when he arrives.
The cart arrives very late, and the coffin is carried into the farmhouse hall. Troy is away from home, and Joseph Poorgrass tells his sad story to Gabriel.
Gabriel reads the words on the lid, which say Fanny Robin and child. He quietly wipes out the last two words, so that gossip will not begin.
A rumour reaches Bathsheba that Fanny had a child and that Troy was the father. She does not want to believe it, but she cannot sleep.
Bathsheba takes a candle and goes softly down the dark stairs. She stands beside the coffin for a long time, and her hands are shaking.
At last Bathsheba lifts the lid and looks inside. She sees Fanny's pale, peaceful face, and beside her lies a tiny baby.
Now Bathsheba understands everything that she has not been told. The baby is Troy's child, and her husband has hidden the truth from her.
While she stands there, the door opens, and Troy comes in. He sees the open coffin and his wife's white face, and all the colour leaves his own.
Troy kneels beside the coffin and kisses Fanny's cold face. He tells Bathsheba that this dead girl meant more to him than she ever did, and then he walks out.
Bathsheba is left alone with the coffin and the last of the candle. She sinks down on the stairs and cries until she falls asleep.
The next day Fanny and her baby are buried in the churchyard at Weatherbury. Only a few people come, and the sky is grey and heavy.
Troy goes to Casterbridge and spends all his money on a fine stone for Fanny's grave. He wants it to carry her name and a few kind words.
Troy takes the stone to the churchyard and plants flowers all over the grave. He works for hours, and by evening the grave looks like a small garden.
That night a very heavy rain begins to fall in the dark. Water rushes from the church roof through a stone spout, and it pours straight onto Fanny's grave.
In the morning Troy finds the flowers washed out and lying in the mud. He feels that even heaven is against him, and he cannot bear to stay.
Troy walks for many hours across the country until he reaches the sea. It is evening, and the little bay of Lulworth Cove is quiet.
Troy takes off his clothes, leaves them on the shore and walks into the water. He swims out strongly, but the current is stronger than he knows.
A boatman finds Troy's clothes on the sand, and the news is carried back to Weatherbury. Everyone there soon believes that the unlucky soldier has drowned.
Bathsheba hears the news and puts on black clothes. She sits alone at her window and lives quietly, as a widow should.
While Bathsheba grieves, Gabriel quietly keeps the farm running. He looks after the sheep, the barns and the accounts, and she begins to rely on him.
At last Bathsheba asks Gabriel to be her bailiff, in charge of all the farm work. He accepts, and the money troubles of the farm slowly begin to improve.
Months pass, and Boldwood comes to see Bathsheba again. He has never stopped loving her, and he begs her to marry him.
Boldwood begs her to promise that she will marry him one day, when the long years are over. He says that he is willing to wait for six years if he must.
Bathsheba does not love him, and she hesitates for a long time. But she remembers the valentine and her own thoughtless joke, and she feels guilty.
At last Bathsheba says that she will marry him after six years, if her husband is never found. It is a sad promise, and she does not want to give it.
Boldwood is happier than he has been in years. He decides to hold a Christmas party for all his neighbours, and he invites Bathsheba.
On Christmas Eve Boldwood's big house shines with candles and green holly. Fires burn in every room, and the long tables are loaded with food.
Bathsheba does not want to go to the party, but Liddy persuades her. She arrives late, in a quiet dress, and Boldwood meets her at the door.
Boldwood takes Bathsheba aside and asks her to promise again. He presses a ring into her hand, and she is too confused to refuse it.
Suddenly the door opens, and a cold wind blows through the warm room. A tall man in a long coat stands in the doorway, and nobody knows him.
The man takes off his hat, and everyone sees with horror that it is Troy. He looks coolly at Bathsheba and tells her to come home with him at once.
Troy strides across the room and seizes Bathsheba by the arm, telling her again to come home. She cries out in fear, and the whole room falls silent.
Boldwood walks across the room to the place where a gun hangs on the wall. His face is white and fixed, and his hands do not shake at all.
Boldwood raises the gun and fires it, and the noise fills the whole house. Troy falls to the floor and dies at once, and the room is filled with screams.
Boldwood puts the gun down and walks calmly out of the house. He does not say a word to anyone, and nobody dares to stop him.
Boldwood walks along the frosty road toward Casterbridge all through the night. At the door of the prison he gives himself up and says what he has done.
A few weeks later Boldwood is tried in the court at Casterbridge. The room is crowded, and everyone is shocked that such a calm man could do such a thing.
Witnesses tell the court that Boldwood has always been a good and honest man. Some say that his mind has been troubled for a very long time.
The jury finds Boldwood guilty, and the judge says that he must be put to death. The court is silent, and Boldwood bows his head quietly.
But the people of the district do not forget his good character. They sign a paper asking for mercy, because they believe that his mind was not well.
At last the news arrives that the sentence has been changed. Boldwood will not die, but he will be kept in prison, and Bathsheba hears it with sorrow.
After the trial Bathsheba shuts herself away in her house. She is pale and silent, and she sees no one for many weeks.
Gabriel runs the farm while Bathsheba is shut away. The villagers stop him on the road and ask how their mistress is.
Then Gabriel makes up his mind to leave Weatherbury. He tells people that he will go to California at the end of the year.
Liddy tells Bathsheba that Gabriel is going away across the sea. Bathsheba is deeply shocked, and for the first time in weeks she begins to cry.
At dusk Bathsheba puts on her shawl and walks across the fields to Gabriel's cottage. She stands at the door for a moment, and then she knocks.
Gabriel opens the door, and his face shows how surprised he is. Bathsheba asks him gently why he is going away.
They talk honestly together, as they have never talked before. Gabriel says that he has always loved her, and that he cannot stay near her and say nothing.
Bathsheba tells him that there is nobody in the world she trusts as she trusts him. Gabriel looks at her for a long time, and then he decides to stay.
Gabriel and Bathsheba are married quietly at the village church, with only a few friends beside them. There is no show and no crowd, because that is what they both want.
That evening the friends gather at the house and sing beneath the windows. The song carries far across the quiet fields, and the long story ends in peace.
C1C2: On Norcombe Hill, a bleak chalk ridge above a sleepy valley, Gabriel Oak tended the modest flock that was the pride of his twenty-eight years. He was a sober, steady young man, careful with money and slow to boast, and he had borrowed a good deal to buy those sheep. Every morning he counted them against the sky and promised himself that one day the flock would grow into a farm.

When the day's work was done, Gabriel would sit on the step of his little wooden hut and play the flute until the stars came out. His old sheepdog lay quietly at his feet, wise and content, while the young one fidgeted at the edge of the light, eager for something to chase. It was a simple life, and he had never thought of wishing for another.

One frosty morning a heavy wagon came creaking along the road beneath the hill, loaded with tables, chairs, a looking-glass and a great many boxes. On top of the pile sat a young woman, surveying the countryside as a queen might survey her kingdom. Gabriel, leaning on his crook, found that he had quite forgotten to count his sheep that morning.

Believing herself quite alone, the girl drew a small mirror from among the furniture and studied her own face with calm, unhurried pleasure. She turned her head this way and that, touched a stray lock of hair, and smiled at what she saw. Gabriel, watching from the hill, laughed softly at her vanity and yet felt something stir in him that was far warmer than amusement.

At the toll gate the keeper held out his hand, and the girl searched her pockets in growing confusion, for she had no coin to give. Gabriel, who had come down the hill to see her better, stepped forward and paid the small fee himself without being asked. He expected at least a smile in return, but no smile and no word of thanks came.

The girl took no more notice of him than if he had been a gatepost, and the wagon rolled on with her chin held high. Gabriel stood in the road, two pence poorer, with the odd feeling that he had been quietly outweighed by a proud young woman. He thought he had never seen anyone so vain, and he knew he would not forget her.

It did not take long for Gabriel to learn what he wished to know, for in a country place nothing stays hidden for long. The girl was Bathsheba Everdene, who had come to live with her aunt at the farm beyond the hill, and she was said to be clever, quick-tempered and as proud as she looked. He turned this news over in his mind many times that day and found that he liked every word of it.

Gabriel chose a small, motherless lamb from his flock, wrapped it in his coat, and carried it down the hill to the aunt's farm. It was an odd sort of gift for a young woman, and he knew it, but it was the best thing he had. All the way across the wet fields he rehearsed what he would say, and each speech sounded worse than the last.

Bathsheba received the lamb with a quick smile and laid it by the kitchen fire, where it bleated for a mother who was not there. She thanked him politely enough, yet her bright eyes laughed at his clumsy speech and his muddy boots. Her aunt, who saw more than she said, invited him to call whenever he liked, and Gabriel went away walking on air.

That night Gabriel climbed the hill beneath a sky crowded with stars and felt quite certain that his life had changed. He was not a man given to sudden fancies, yet he knew, as plainly as he knew his own flock, that he had found the woman he meant to marry. It did not once cross his mind that she might refuse him when he asked.

In the weeks that followed, Gabriel found that he could think of nothing but Bathsheba, not even when he was counting the flock or mending a hurdle in the rain. He made small mistakes that were quite unlike him, and the old dog watched him with a puzzled, patient look. At last he saw that there was only one cure for his trouble, and that was to ask the girl herself.

On a bright, blustery morning Gabriel took out his best coat, brushed it carefully, and washed his face in the cold water of the stream. He tried to smooth down his stubborn hair and practised a few sensible sentences in front of the dogs, who were not at all impressed. Then, with the air of a man going to meet his fate, he set off down the hill.

The fields were wet and the lane was thick with mud, but Gabriel noticed nothing of it as he went, for his whole mind was fixed on what he meant to say. When he reached the farm he found Bathsheba alone beside a gate, with the low sun behind her and a bright colour in her cheeks. She looked so lovely that every sensible sentence he had prepared flew out of his head.

Gabriel told her plainly that he loved her and that he wished with all his heart to have her for his wife. He was only a small farmer, he said, but he would work for her every day of his life, and she should have a comfortable home and even a piano of her own. He spoke gravely, as he did about everything, and it never occurred to him to dress his offer in pretty words.

Bathsheba heard him to the end, and then she shook her head with a small, kind, unmistakable smile. She said that she did not love him, and that what she wanted was a husband who could tame her, which was a thing he would never be able to do. It was said so lightly that for a moment he hardly understood that he had been refused.

Gabriel pleaded that he would love her faithfully for as long as he lived, and that she would never find a man who would cherish her more. Bathsheba only stepped back, and her voice grew sharp as she said that she hated the very thought of being anyone's property. He saw then that no argument of his could turn her, and that the more he begged, the further away she would go.

He begged her at least not to be angry with him, but she only gave him a quick, restless glance and walked away along the lane. Gabriel stood quite still beside the gate with his hat in his hands and watched her until the hedge hid her from view. A great silence seemed to settle over the whole valley, and Gabriel felt very small beneath it.

A few days later Gabriel heard that Bathsheba had quietly left the district, and no one in the village could say where she had gone. He asked as casually as he could, and was answered only with rumours and shrugs. It seemed that the proud girl had walked clean out of his life, and had taken the best part of the spring with her.

Gabriel went back to his flock and told himself, with great firmness, that a sensible man ought to forget what he could not have. It was excellent advice, and he gave it to himself many times a day, but it proved far easier to give than to follow. He worked from dawn until dark, and by night he was too tired to dream of anyone.

When lambing time came, the hill was crowded with ewes and tiny, wobbling lambs, and Gabriel hardly slept for a fortnight. He lost very few, and the farmers of the district began to say that the young shepherd was careful, honest and cleverer than his years. His flock grew steadily, and for a while he almost believed that he was happy.

Gabriel's old sheepdog was a creature of great sense, who understood the flock as well as its master did and never ran when a walk would do. The young dog was quite another matter, for it was strong, quick and bursting with joy, and it had never learned that sheep are not to be frightened. Gabriel loved it all the same, and he trusted it a little more than he ought.

One night, after a long week of lambing in which he had scarcely closed his eyes, Gabriel crept into his hut for a short rest. The wind had dropped, the sheep lay quiet in the moonlight, and the old dog sat watching beside the door. Before he had counted a hundred breaths, he was fast asleep, and the whole hill was in the keeping of two dogs.

Outside the hut the moon rode high, and the sheep lay quiet on the cold grass until the young dog suddenly sprang to its feet. It had never been shown how to herd, and it knew only that sheep were meant to be run after, and that running was wonderful. In a moment the whole hillside was filled with the patter of small hooves.

The terrified flock streamed across the hill like a grey river in the dark, with the young dog barking joyfully at its heels. The old dog sent up a warning bark that rang across the slope, but nothing could stop the animals now, for they were blind with fear. Ahead of them, hidden in the long grass, lay the edge of an old chalk pit.

The leaders reached the edge of the pit and could not stop, for the sheep behind them pressed on without seeing the drop. One after another they went over and fell into the dark, with a sound that the night quickly swallowed. By the time the young dog understood what it had done, the hill was silent and empty.

Gabriel woke at dawn with a vague sense that something was wrong, and he stepped out of the hut into a pale, cold light. The field where his flock had lain was bare, trampled and silent, and only the old dog came to meet him, whining. He followed the marks of the hooves across the hill, and his heart grew heavier at every step.

At the lip of the chalk pit Gabriel stopped, and for a long moment he could not bring himself to look down. When he did, he saw his whole flock lying broken at the bottom, the work of years undone in a single night. He stood there without a word, and knew that he had lost nearly everything he owned.

He found the young dog crouching in the grass, ashamed and bewildered, for it had no notion of the harm it had done. Gabriel did not blame the creature, which had only followed its nature, yet it could never again be trusted near a flock. It was a sad and bitter task, but the dog had to be put down that morning.

Gabriel had borrowed a large part of the money to buy his flock, and no insurance stood between him and the loss. His creditors were fair men, but they wanted what they were owed, and there was only one way to pay it. He sold his tools, his hurdles and his lease, and he asked no one for pity.

When the last bill was paid and the last cart had rolled away, Gabriel stood in the empty field and looked about him. He who had been a master was a master no longer, and all that he possessed in the world was a crook, a flute and a little money. Yet he did not complain, for he was a man who bore his troubles in silence.

Early one grey morning Gabriel took a last look at the hill where he had been happy, and then he turned his back on it. He carried his few possessions in a bundle over his shoulder, with his crook in one hand and his flute tucked into his coat. The days of owning a flock were over, and he meant to find work as a plain farm hand.

The hiring fair at Casterbridge was a strange, crowded sight, for the labourers of the whole county stood about the market place in rows, waiting to be chosen. Each man carried the sign of his trade, so that the shepherds held their crooks, the carters twists of whipcord and the thatchers a wisp of straw in their hats. Farmers walked slowly along the lines, looking the men over as they might have looked over cattle.

Gabriel took his place among the shepherds, holding his crook as the others did, and he stood there from early morning until the shadows grew long. Farmers looked him over, asked a question or two, and passed on, for there were more shepherds than places, and he had no master to speak for him. It was a humbling thing for a man who had so lately been his own employer.

When the lamps were lit and the crowd began to thin, Gabriel was still without a master, and the market place looked suddenly cold and empty. He ate the last of his bread, shouldered his bundle and decided to try his luck in another town. The road ahead was dark, but he had known darker nights on the hill.

Tired out, he climbed into a wagon loaded with hay that stood by the roadside, and in a few moments he was asleep. He woke with a start in the middle of the night and saw, far across the dark fields, an angry red glow that flickered and leaped against the clouds. Without stopping to think, he jumped down from the wagon and began to run toward the fire.

He arrived at a farm where the great stacks of hay were burning fiercely, throwing sparks high into the black sky and lighting every face in the yard. The workers ran this way and that, shouting and beating at the flames with their coats, but nobody had taken charge, and the fire was winning. A barn full of corn stood close beside the nearest stack, and its roof had begun to smoke.

Gabriel saw at a glance that the men were not working but merely running, and that someone must give orders at once. In a clear, calm voice, which none of them thought of questioning, he sent them for water and wet sacks and told others to drag the burning straw away from the stacks. Within a few minutes the shouting crowd had become a steady line of workers.

Gabriel climbed to the top of the largest stack, where the heat was fiercest and a single falling spark could undo all his work. He beat out the flames with a wet sack, shouted for more water, and stayed there while the men below passed up bucket after bucket. His face was black and his coat was scorched, but he did not give an inch.

At last the flames sank into smoke, and the stacks that remained stood dark and wet and safe against the paling sky. The workers dropped to the ground in their blackened shirts, too weary to speak, and more than one looked up at the stranger with frank admiration. Gabriel sat down among them, aching in every limb, and wondered whose farm he had saved.

As the first light of morning crept over the yard, a young woman in a long shawl came slowly toward the weary men through the thinning smoke. She was the owner of the farm, it seemed, and she had come out to learn who had saved her harvest. Gabriel got to his feet, and the first sight of her face made him forget his tiredness.

As she came closer, Gabriel knew her face before she had spoken a word, and his tiredness fell away in a moment. It was Bathsheba Everdene, the proud girl who had refused him on Norcombe Hill, now the mistress of this farm, which she had inherited from her uncle. He drew his hat a little lower over his blackened face and waited, hoping that she would not see who he was.

Bathsheba thanked the stranger warmly for his help and asked, in a clear, businesslike voice, whether there was anything that she could do for him. Gabriel answered that he was a shepherd by trade, that he had lately lost his own flock, and that he was looking for a place. She seemed to study him for a moment, though whether she knew him he could not tell.

Bathsheba told him that she badly needed a good shepherd, and that she would take him on at once if he was willing to begin that day. Gabriel said that he was willing, and he said it with perfect calm, as if he had never seen her before in his life. So it was that the young farmer who had once offered her a piano now took wages from her as her shepherd.

A cheerful young maid called Liddy Smallbury brought Gabriel bread, cheese and a mug of milk, and watched him eat with open curiosity. She was a great talker, and before he had finished his meal he knew the names of the workers, the troubles of the dairy and the exact moods of her mistress. He listened gravely, thanked her, and slept better than he had slept for many a night.

The next morning Bathsheba called every man and woman on the farm into the yard and stood before them with her head high. She told them quietly that there would be no bailiff in future, because she meant to manage the farm herself, and that she expected honest work from everyone. A few of the men exchanged doubtful looks, but nobody dared to say a word against her that morning.

Then she turned to Pennyways, the bailiff who had managed the farm under her uncle, and told him in an even voice that she had found out how he had been robbing her. He protested, blustered and swore that he was innocent, but she was not to be moved. In a quarter of an hour he had gone, with his bundle under his arm and his career in ruins.

The workers watched Pennyways stride away down the lane, and for a while nobody said anything at all. Some of them were secretly impressed by the young mistress, who had dismissed a man twice her age without raising her voice, while others muttered that a woman had no business running a farm. Gabriel kept his thoughts to himself and went quietly off to see to the sheep on the hill.

From that day Bathsheba rose before the workers and walked around her fields, barns and sheep pens, asking sharp questions about everything she saw. In the evenings she sat over her account books by candlelight until the figures stood in neat, honest rows. The farm had never been so closely watched, and Gabriel, who knew a good farmer when he saw one, could not help admiring her.

In the evenings the workers of Weatherbury gathered in the old malthouse, where the glow of the kiln lit their faces and a cask of cider went from hand to hand. Jan Coggan, Joseph Poorgrass, Mark Clark, Henery Fray and young Cainy Ball sat there as they had sat for years, settling the affairs of the parish without ever being asked. Nothing could happen on the farm that was not turned over, slowly and thoroughly, in that warm room.

When Gabriel came in out of the dark, the talk stopped for a moment while the old men looked him over with slow, friendly curiosity. He sat down on the settle, accepted a mug of cider and said very little, which was exactly the right thing to say. Before the evening was out, the men had decided that the new shepherd was a good sort, and they were telling him everything.

One evening the talk in the malthouse turned to Fanny Robin, a slight, quiet girl who had worked on the farm until she vanished without a word. Nobody knew where she had gone, but several of the men shook their heads and said that a soldier was at the bottom of it, and a handsome one at that. Gabriel listened in silence, with the sympathy of a man who knew what it was to lose something.

Henery Fray grumbled bitterly that he had served the farm for many years and ought to have been made bailiff in Pennyways's place. Old Jan Coggan only laughed at him, and declared that the new mistress had more sense in her little finger than all the men in the room put together. The fire crackled, the cider went round, and the argument went on, as it did every night.

It was late when Gabriel left the malthouse, and the road home ran dark and cold between its dripping hedges. The wind moaned in the trees, there was no moon, and the sound of his own boots was the only company he had. Then, from the shadow of a gatepost, a small, shaking voice asked him to stop.

A slight figure stepped out of the shadows, pale as paper and wrapped in a thin shawl, and Gabriel saw by the faint starlight that it was Fanny Robin. She was shivering, and her eyes were red with weeping, and she looked like a creature who had walked a long way without hope. He asked her gently what he could do, and what had brought her out alone on such a night.

Fanny told him in a trembling whisper that she was on her way to Casterbridge, where she was to be married to a soldier, but that she had no money left for the journey. She begged him to help her, and she begged still harder that he would tell no one at the farm that he had seen her. There was such terror in her voice that Gabriel did not think of asking why.

Gabriel emptied his pockets into her hand, giving her every coin that he possessed, though it left him almost as poor as when he had come to Weatherbury. Fanny whispered her thanks, wiped her eyes on the end of her shawl and hurried off in the direction of Casterbridge. He stood for a long while listening to her footsteps, until the dark took them away.

The soldier whom Fanny loved was Sergeant Frank Troy, who was stationed at the barracks in Casterbridge, and who was as handsome as he was careless. He had flattered her, laughed with her and promised to make her his wife, and she had believed every word. She had left the farm in the night, because she was sure that her whole happiness depended upon it.

On the morning that was to have been her wedding day, Fanny put on her best dress, pinned up her hair and hurried through the streets to the church. Her heart was beating fast, for she was terribly afraid of being late, and she did not stop to ask anyone the way. She found a church with its doors open, and she went inside to wait.

But Fanny had gone to All Saints, and Troy, who was waiting at All Souls, stood at the altar in his scarlet coat with his friends beside him. The clock moved on, the minutes dragged, and nobody came to marry him, while she sat alone in the wrong church and knew nothing of her mistake. When at last she learned the truth, it was already too late to put it right.

Troy was furious, and, far worse, he was humiliated, for the whole barracks would laugh at the bridegroom who had been left standing at the church. He would not forgive her, and he would not listen, and her tears only made him colder. Fanny was left alone in the street, with no wedding, no money and nowhere in the world to go.

On market day Bathsheba drove into Casterbridge to sell her corn, a bold thing for a young woman to do, since the corn market was a world of men. She walked among the crowded stalls with her head high and her eyes bright, exactly as if she had been doing it all her life. The farmers made way for her, looked at one another, and muttered that the old farmer's niece had a great deal of spirit.

Every head in the market turned as she passed, and the buzz of bargaining died away into a murmur of admiration. Bathsheba pretended not to notice, but she noticed everything, and she could not help being pleased by such a harvest of glances. It was a pleasure she had known since she was a girl, and she had never tired of it.

Only one man in the whole market did not turn his head, and that was William Boldwood, a tall, grave, prosperous farmer of about forty, who stood a little apart with his back toward her. He seemed to be thinking of nothing but his own affairs, and he moved away without so much as a glance. Bathsheba felt a small, sharp sting of annoyance that she could not quite account for.

On the road home Bathsheba asked Liddy, as carelessly as she could, who the man was who had not looked at her. Liddy answered that he was Farmer Boldwood, the richest bachelor in the parish, who was said never to have cared for a woman in his life. This was precisely the wrong thing to tell a girl who liked to be admired.

On Valentine's Day, with a long evening before them and nothing to do, Bathsheba and Liddy found a pretty card with a verse printed on it. Liddy, who loved a joke as much as her mistress, suggested that they should send it to someone, and the more unlikely the person, the better. Bathsheba laughed, and the idea took hold of her at once, as ideas do when one is bored and young.

Liddy proposed little Teddy Coggan, a small, solemn boy of the village, but Bathsheba wanted a bigger joke than that. At last she said that they would leave it to fate, and that they would toss a hymn-book, so that if it fell open the card would go to Farmer Boldwood. She did not truly expect it to fall that way, but she was a girl who loved a dare.

Bathsheba tossed the book into the air, and it came down on the floor and lay open, as if it had always meant to. The two girls stared at each other and then burst out laughing, for it was a joke that nobody could have planned. The card, it was settled, would go to the one man in the parish who had not looked at her.

Bathsheba took a stick of red sealing wax from the writing desk and warmed it in the flame of the candle. Liddy looked on, giggling, as she pressed the seal onto the fold of the card, and the soft wax took the print of two small words, Marry me. It was only a joke, and neither of them gave a moment's thought to the weight of it.

Liddy laughed until she could scarcely stand, and Bathsheba, a little breathless herself, wrote Farmer Boldwood's name on the outside in a bold hand. The card was given to a boy and sent off through the dusk to the quiet house on the other side of the parish. Neither of them dreamed of what it would set moving, or of how many lives it would turn upside down.

At breakfast the next morning Boldwood found among his letters a small card, sealed with red wax and addressed in a hand that he did not know. He broke the seal with a steady finger, and he read the two words beneath it once, and then again. In forty years nobody had ever said such a thing to him, even in jest.

Boldwood propped the card against the clock on his mantelpiece, as a man might set up a puzzle that he meant to solve before night. All that day he found himself returning to it, picking it up, turning it over and wondering who had written those two bold words. His farm ran as it always ran, but his mind had quietly left it.

On Sunday in church, Boldwood, who had never in his life lifted his eyes toward the women's pews, turned his head and looked at Bathsheba. She kept her gaze fixed upon her prayer-book, but a deep colour rose in her cheeks, for she could feel his stare like a hand upon her shoulder. It was the first time that any man had made her afraid of her own joke.

Boldwood could not sleep, and night after night he walked up and down his quiet house, listening to the wind. He had always believed that his heart was a still, deep lake, which no weather could ruffle, but the card had fallen into it like a stone. By the end of the week he was no longer curious about the girl who had sent it, for he was in love with her.

At last he put on his best coat and rode over to Bathsheba's farm, with the grave, set face of a man going into battle. His manner was calm, as it always was, but his heart was beating so loudly that he fancied his horse must hear it. He tied the animal at the gate and walked up the path to her door.

Boldwood spoke to Bathsheba at her door in a quiet, serious voice, as a man speaks when he has thought about his words for a week. He told her that her valentine had changed his life, that he loved her more than he could say, and that he asked her to be his wife. There was no flattery in his manner, only a deep and solemn earnestness that frightened her.

Bathsheba, shaken to the heart, told him honestly that she did not love him and had never thought of such a thing. Yet she could not bring herself to refuse a man who spoke so humbly, and who looked so deeply wounded at the thought of it, and she promised that she would consider his offer. Boldwood thanked her gravely and went away, glowing like a man who has been given a kingdom.

When he had gone, Bathsheba sat down alone and felt ashamed, for her joke had grown into something that she had not meant and could not easily undo. She did not love Boldwood, and she did not wish to marry him, yet she had given him hope, and hope in such a man was a heavy thing to take back. For the first time in her life she wished that she had not been so clever.

Before long the whole parish was talking about the visit, and the men in the malthouse told Gabriel all that they knew, and a good deal that they did not. Gabriel heard the tale of the valentine in silence, and he thought that it was the kind of joke that a girl tells who has never been hurt herself. He decided that someone ought to say so, and that no one else would dare.

Gabriel found Bathsheba in the farmyard and told her plainly, with his hat in his hand, that her valentine had been a thoughtless and unkind thing to do. Boldwood was not a man to be played with, he said, and a joke that was only a joke to her might be a wound to him. His voice was gentle, but he did not soften a single word of what he had come to say.

Bathsheba's face went scarlet, and she told him in a voice that shook with anger that he was impertinent, and that it was no business of his what she did. She added, with cold and quivering dignity, that he might leave her service that very hour. Gabriel bowed his head, said that he was sorry, and turned away without another word.

Gabriel packed his few belongings, shook hands with the astonished workers in the yard and walked out of the farm gate at dawn. Nobody wished to see him go, for in a short time he had made himself the best man on the place, but he did not once look back. Behind him the sheep stood on the hill with no one to watch them.

A few days later the flock found a gap in the fence and rushed into a field of fresh young clover, which no shepherd had thought to guard. They ate greedily, as hungry animals will, and none of the boys who should have been watching them noticed what was happening. By the time anyone looked up, the damage was already done, and the field was strangely quiet.

Fresh clover is among the most dangerous foods in the world for a sheep, for it fills the animal with gas until its sides swell like a drum. Within an hour the ewes were staggering, then lying down, and then, one by one, beginning to die. The workers who ran out to the field had never seen anything like it, and they had no idea what to do.

Bathsheba, summoned in haste, ran down to the field with her skirts held up and her hair half blown loose. What she saw there made her cry out, for the ewes lay swollen on the grass, and the men stood about them with their hands hanging uselessly at their sides. Every minute that she stood there, another sheep was lost, and every man there knew it as well as she.

It was old Jan Coggan who remembered the shepherd who had gone, and a boy was sent running across the fields to find him. Gabriel had not yet left the neighbourhood, and the boy, red-faced and gasping, poured out the whole story of the clover. Gabriel listened with a grave face and said that he would not go back unless the mistress herself asked him.

When she heard what he had said, Bathsheba did what she had never done before in her life, and swallowed her pride. She went to him herself, with her colour high and her voice unsteady, and begged him to come back and save her sheep. Gabriel did not make her ask twice, and they hurried together to the field.

Gabriel drew from his pocket a small, sharp, hollow instrument that he had carried for years, and knelt beside the nearest swollen ewe. With one swift, steady movement he pierced her side, and the gas rushed out with a hiss that made the watching men start back. The ewe shivered, and then she lifted her head and breathed freely, as if she had been let out of a prison.

Gabriel went from ewe to ewe, kneeling, piercing, rising and moving on, while the workers stood in silent wonder and Bathsheba held up the lantern. Many of the sheep recovered at once and struggled to their feet, shaking themselves in the dusk. It was a long, hard task, and a few were too far gone to be saved.

When the last sheep had been seen to, Bathsheba stood before him, tired and tearful, and thanked him as she had never thanked anyone. She told him that she could not do without him and asked him to stay, and her pride lay quite forgotten in the grass behind her. It was the nearest thing to an apology that she was ever likely to make.

Gabriel said that he would stay, and he said it simply, as though the whole quarrel had never been. The men of the farm, who had watched him work that day, regarded him now as little less than a wizard, and they told the story in the malthouse for months afterwards. As for Gabriel, he was only glad that he might stay near her, though he knew that he must say nothing of his love.

In early summer the sheep were driven down to the river and washed, one by one, in a deep pool beneath the willows, so that their wool would be clean for shearing. The men stood waist-deep in the cold water, shouting and laughing, while Bathsheba watched from the bank with her shawl over her arm. It was the busiest and merriest day of the farm's year, and the whole parish seemed to have gathered to enjoy it.

In the middle of the morning Boldwood rode up to the pool and dismounted, saying something about a matter of business that nobody believed. He stood on the bank with his hat in his hand, watching Bathsheba as a thirsty man watches water, and he did not once glance at the sheep. The workers nudged one another with knowing looks, and Bathsheba felt the weight of his gaze upon her like a hand.

Gabriel, standing in the water with a struggling ewe in his arms, saw the look on Boldwood's face and understood it better than anyone there. He had worn that look himself on Norcombe Hill, and he knew how little it had availed him. He said nothing, for it was not his place to speak, but he bent over the sheep with a heavy heart.

A few days later the shearing began in the great barn, a vast, dim, cathedral-like building with a roof of ancient timbers and a floor worn smooth by generations of boots. The air was warm and heavy with the smell of wool, and the shears clicked in rows from morning to night. Gabriel was the quickest and neatest of all the shearers, and the fleeces piled up beside him like drifts of snow.

When the last fleece was off, a long table was laid in the barn for the shearing supper, and it groaned beneath the weight of cold meat, bread, cheese and cider. Lanterns hung from the beams, the old songs began, and the whole company sat down in the glow with the satisfaction of people who have worked well. It was the evening of the year when mistress and workers sat together at one table.

Boldwood arrived late, hat in hand, and Bathsheba, who could hardly refuse him, asked him to take the seat beside her at the head of the table. She was gracious, but she was also nervous, for she knew very well why he had come, and she felt a hundred eyes upon her. The songs went on around them as if nothing were happening, and the lanterns swung gently in the draught from the great doors.

When the singing grew loud and the cider had made the company cheerful, Boldwood leaned toward her and spoke in a low voice that nobody else could hear. He asked her for the answer that she had promised him, saying that he had thought of nothing else since the day of the valentine. His patience, he told her, was real, but it was not without an end.

Bathsheba, who had no wish to answer him before a hundred listeners, said gently that he should have his answer before long, and begged him not to press her tonight. Boldwood bowed his head and said that he could wait a little longer, and that it was not for him to complain. He sat very still for the rest of the evening, like a man listening for a distant bell.

A few evenings later Bathsheba walked out alone across her fields in the gathering dark, as she liked to do when her mind was full. The air was soft and warm, the hedges smelled of honeysuckle, and her thoughts went round and round Boldwood's question without finding an answer. She had no notion that anyone was near her, and she would have laughed at the idea that this quiet evening could change her life.

To shorten her way home she turned into a plantation of fir trees, where the darkness was so thick that she could scarcely see her own hand. The path was narrow and soft with fallen needles, and the branches stirred overhead with a sound like the sea. Somewhere ahead, in the blackness, a twig cracked sharply, and she stopped still with her heart beating in her ears.

In the black of the wood Bathsheba walked straight into a man who was coming the other way, and she cried out in alarm. She tried to step back, but her skirt had caught fast on something that glittered faintly, and the harder she pulled, the tighter it held. The stranger, who did not seem alarmed in the least, began to laugh, softly and with evident enjoyment.

It was the spur of a soldier's boot that held her, and the man himself, who seemed in no hurry to set her free, made a great show of untangling the cloth in the dark. He apologised in a smooth, easy voice that was full of amusement, and the more he apologised, the more the dress seemed to cling. Bathsheba, who was not accustomed to being laughed at, felt her temper rise and her cheeks grow hot in the darkness.

The soldier opened a small lantern, and the sudden light fell on a young, bold, handsome face and a coat of brilliant scarlet. He looked at Bathsheba for a long moment with unconcealed admiration, and she, who was used to making men look at her, found herself blushing. She had never been so thoroughly looked at in her life, and she did not know whether to be angry or flattered.

He told her that he was Sergeant Troy of the barracks at Casterbridge, and that he begged her pardon for the accident, which he could not find it in his heart to regret. She was, he assured her, the most beautiful woman he had ever seen, and he had seen a good many. Bathsheba knew perfectly well that this was flattery, and she liked it more than she cared to admit.

At last the dress was free, and Bathsheba, with a hasty word of thanks and a high, offended manner, hurried away along the path. Behind her she could hear the soldier laughing softly, and she told herself that she was furious with him. By the time she reached her own door, she had quite forgotten to be.

The next afternoon, to Bathsheba's great surprise, Troy strolled into the hayfield in his shirt-sleeves, took a rake from one of the men and set to work beside her. He was idle and charming by turns, and he made the labourers laugh with his stories of barracks and battles. Gabriel, raking hay at the other end of the field with a very quiet face, did not laugh at all.

When the work was done, Troy asked her whether she had ever seen the sword exercise, which he said was the finest thing a soldier could show to a lady. She answered that she had not, and that she doubted whether it was proper to see it, but her curiosity won the argument. They agreed to meet at a quiet hollow in the fields at sundown, and they agreed to tell nobody.

At sundown Bathsheba came to the hollow, a deep, green, secret place, full of ferns that reached to her waist and hidden from every path in the parish. Troy was waiting there, bareheaded, with a long sword in his hand, and the last of the sunlight ran along the blade like a stream of fire. She wondered, a little late, whether she ought to have come, and whether a respectable woman would have stayed.

Troy told her to stand perfectly still and trust him, and then he began to move, and the sword became a shining blur in the evening air. It whirled about her head, her shoulders and her waist, so close that she felt the wind of it, and yet it never touched her. Bathsheba stood spellbound, breathless between terror and delight, and she did not once think of moving away.

With a final flourish he sliced off a single curl of her hair, caught it on the point of his sword and presented it to her with a bow. Bathsheba was frightened, thrilled and dazzled all at once, and she knew that nothing in her quiet, clever life had prepared her for this man. She walked home through the dusk as if in a dream, with her heart racing and her cheeks on fire.

Bathsheba went about her work in a dream, smiling at nothing, forgetting her accounts and hardly tasting her dinner. Liddy, who watched her mistress with the sharp eyes of a girl who loves a secret, saw at once what was the matter. The proud woman who had refused a good farmer and laughed at a rich one had lost her heart to a scarlet coat.

Soon the men in the malthouse were talking of nothing but the soldier and their mistress, and Gabriel heard it all with a growing sense of dread. He had seen Troy's kind of charm before, and he knew that it was a bright but shallow thing. At last he made up his mind that, whatever it cost him, he would say what he thought.

Gabriel found Bathsheba in the farmyard and spoke to her gravely, with his eyes on the ground, as one who knows that he is risking a good deal. He told her that Sergeant Troy was not a good man, that he was careless of other people's feelings, and that he would bring her sorrow. It was a hard speech to make to a woman who had once refused him, and he made it without the smallest hope of thanks.

Bathsheba was pale with indignation, and she said that he had no right to speak so of a man whom he scarcely knew, and no right to speak at all. She told him that if he did not like her way of managing her own affairs he was free to go, and she turned her back upon him. Gabriel did not go, and he did not say another word, but he stood by the gate for a long time after she had vanished.

The same story soon reached Boldwood, who had been waiting patiently at home for the answer that he had been promised. At first he refused to believe that the woman whom he loved could prefer a careless soldier to a man of his own steady character, but the tale came to him again and again. At last he could bear it no longer, and he went out to look for Troy.

One dark night Boldwood met the soldier on the road, and, stepping out of the shadows, he caught him by the arm in a grip that made Troy stop short. The two men stood there in the wind, the one tall, grave and trembling, the other lounging and half amused. Neither of them could have said how long the silence lasted, and the wind in the hedges seemed to hold its breath.

Boldwood, forgetting his pride, begged Troy to leave Bathsheba alone and to go back to his duties, saying that he loved her with his whole heart and that the soldier's attentions could only end in her unhappiness. He spoke with a passion that would have moved any other man, and his voice broke more than once. He had never begged anyone for anything before, and it cost him more than any loss that he had ever suffered.

But Troy only laughed, a light, careless laugh that cut Boldwood to the quick, and told him that he was a fine fellow and ought to go home and be sensible. He said that a woman had a right to choose for herself, and that it was not for a farmer to give orders to a sergeant. Then he shook off the grip as if it had been a fly, and strolled away whistling into the dark.

Within a few days Troy had gone to the city of Bath, whether on duty or for his own amusement nobody at Weatherbury could tell. He said no farewell to Bathsheba, left no message, and promised nothing, as though the whole summer had been a game that he had grown tired of. Boldwood breathed more easily, and the village waited to see what would happen next.

When Bathsheba heard that he had gone, her high spirits deserted her, and for two days she could neither work nor eat nor sleep. Her pride told her that she ought to forget him and be thankful, but her heart, which had never been used to disobedience, would not listen. On the third morning she gave her orders for the farm, put on her bonnet and set out for Bath.

After a long, jolting journey Bathsheba reached Bath, a handsome city of pale stone, crowded streets and fashionable strangers. She had never been so far from her fields in her life, and she felt very small and very foolish as she stood on the pavement with her bag. It was a long time since she had needed to ask anyone for help.

At last, by the luckiest chance, she saw Troy walking along a street, tall and bright in his scarlet coat, and he stopped dead when he saw her face. For a moment he looked astonished, and then the old charming smile spread over his features, and he took both her hands in his. She forgot at once every word that she had meant to say, and every reproach that she had prepared on the long road.

Troy told her, with every appearance of passion, that he had thought of nothing but her since he left and that he could not live without her. He was too impatient, he said, to wait for the world's approval, and he proposed that they should marry at once, before anyone could come between them. Bathsheba, who ought to have known better, listened with her heart in her mouth.

A cool voice at the back of Bathsheba's mind told her that she was being very foolish, and that she scarcely knew this man. But she had always done exactly as she pleased, and she was in love. She was also a very long way from home, and so in the end, with a hurried and uncertain heart, she gave him the answer that he wanted.

They were married in a quiet church in Bath, with no friends, no family and no guests, and nobody in Weatherbury had the least idea of it. The service was short, the church was cold, and when it was over Bathsheba, who had meant to be the mistress of her own life, was a wife. She wondered, with a small chill, what exactly she had done, and whether she would be able to undo it.

A few days later the couple travelled back to Weatherbury together, and as the familiar fields came into view, Bathsheba grew quieter and quieter. She was proud of her handsome husband and happy to be with him, yet she dreaded the faces of her workers and the opinions of the parish. Troy, who dreaded nothing at all, whistled all the way and admired the farm as if it were already his own.

That evening Bathsheba called all the workers into the yard, and she stood in the lamplight with her new husband at her side. She told them in a clear, unsteady voice that she had been married at Bath and that she was now Mrs Troy, and that the farm would go on as before. Nobody spoke at first, for nobody could think of a single suitable thing to say to a mistress who had gone away single and come back married.

The workers were astonished, and they said very little, but that night the malthouse hummed like a hive. Old Jan Coggan thought it a bold match, Henery Fray predicted trouble, and Joseph Poorgrass said, with a sigh, that it was a hard world for a woman who would not be told. The sergeant, meanwhile, strolled round the farm as if he had been born to own it.

Gabriel heard the news without a word and went on with his work as if nothing had happened, but a stranger would have seen how slowly his hands moved. He had warned her, and he had been right to warn her, yet he found that he took no pleasure in being right. The best that he could do for her now was to stay, and to watch, and to wait.

When the tidings reached Boldwood, they struck him like a blow upon the heart, and for a time he could not speak or move. He shut himself away in his great silent house, ate almost nothing, and saw no one, while the corn ripened unregarded in his fields. In the quiet of those days something in him was slowly and dangerously beginning to change.

Troy took charge of the farm with the airy confidence of a man who has never been shown his own ignorance, and he gave orders in the barrack-yard voice that had served him so well in the army. He knew nothing about crops or cattle, and the workers, who did know, obeyed him sullenly and shook their heads behind his back. Bathsheba, being in love, thought it all rather charming, and she would not hear a word against him.

Troy was fond of racing, and he spent his days at the races near Casterbridge, betting on horses with the confidence of one who believed that luck was a kind of talent. He wagered Bathsheba's money as freely as if it were his own, and he lost a great deal of it. When she asked him where it had gone, he kissed her and changed the subject.

Bathsheba, who had once known every penny of her accounts, saw with growing alarm that the money was draining away faster than it was earned. She said little, for she was proud and he was her husband, but at night she lay awake and listened to the clock. A shadow had fallen on her happiness, and it was growing larger every week.

The harvest had been brought in, and the great stacks stood in the rick-yard waiting to be thatched, which was a task that could not safely be delayed. Troy, who understood nothing of such things, announced instead that there should be a harvest supper in the barn, and that every man should drink to his heart's content. The workers, who liked the idea of a supper much better than the work of thatching, cheered him loudly and at once.

At the supper Troy poured brandy for every man in the barn and laughed uproariously at their songs, and the more they drank, the louder and sleepier they grew. One after another they slid from their benches and lay snoring on the floor, until the only man in the room who could stand was Gabriel, who had been careful to drink very little. Troy himself had fallen asleep in his chair, flushed and smiling, with his glass still in his hand.
