Outside the barn, Gabriel read the signs that every shepherd learns: a toad crawling across the path, slugs creeping toward the house, the sheep huddled together in a corner of the field, and a thick, brassy stillness in the air. There was going to be a storm, and a bad one, and the great stacks stood in the yard uncovered. If the rain reached the corn before he covered it, the whole harvest would be ruined.

Gabriel hurried back and tried to rouse the men, shaking and shouting, but not one of them could be woken, and Troy lay beyond all calling. There was no one left to do the work, and he decided that he would do it alone, if he had to, with his own two hands. Then he heard a light step behind him, and Bathsheba stood there in the lantern light.

The first thunder rolled across the sky like a loaded cart, and a great wind rose in the dark and tore at the hedges. Gabriel and Bathsheba dragged the heavy covers from the barn and hauled them over the stacks, while the lanterns swung and guttered and threatened to go out. It was heavy work for two people, and the storm was already upon them.

The lightning came faster and brighter, turning the whole rick-yard white and then black again, and the rain began to fall in great cold drops. Bathsheba held the ladder and handed up the ropes, her hair streaming, while Gabriel climbed from stack to stack, tying down the covers and trying not to look at the sky. Each flash seemed to be aimed at him, and each time the thunder followed so closely that the ground shook.

By morning the storm had rolled away, the sky was washed clean and pale, and every stack in the yard stood dry beneath its cover. Bathsheba thanked Gabriel in a low voice that said more than the words, and then she walked slowly toward the barn, where her husband still lay sleeping in his chair. She looked at him for a long moment, and for the first time she saw him as he truly was.

Fanny was ill and weak, and she had neither money nor friends nor any hope left in the world. She resolved at last to walk to the workhouse at Casterbridge, the grim building where the poor of the town were given a bed and a little bread, and to ask for shelter there. It was a long way for a woman in her condition, and the day was bitterly cold.

She walked mile after mile along the lonely road, resting at every milestone and leaning on the hedges when her strength failed. The wind was keen, the afternoon was darkening, and she was so tired that the road seemed to swim before her eyes. Still she went on, because there was nowhere else for her to go, and because stopping would have meant lying down in the cold.

Out of the dusk there came a large dog that trotted up beside her, looked into her face and then walked on at her side as if it understood everything. When she faltered, it waited, and when she leaned upon it, it stood patiently and bore her weight. In that kindly company she found a little more strength than she had thought she possessed.

At last, when the lamps were being lit in the town, Fanny reached the gate of the workhouse and knocked on it with the little strength that remained to her. The door was opened, kind hands took her in, and she was laid on a bed, too weary to give more than her name. The dog, having brought her to safety, stood for a moment in the lamplight and then trotted away into the dark of the night.

Fanny died there before morning, quietly and without a complaint, and her newborn child died with her. She had been a young woman with a gentle heart and a hard fortune, and there was nobody at her bedside who had known her. Of all the lives that Troy's carelessness had touched, hers was the first to be broken beyond mending.

The news reached Weatherbury the next day, and it was arranged that poor Fanny should be brought home and buried in the churchyard of the parish where she had lived. A farm cart was sent to Casterbridge to fetch the coffin, and the task of driving it fell to the gentle and timid Joseph Poorgrass. He set out in good heart, and with a very solemn face, determined to do his duty by the poor girl at last.

Joseph Poorgrass was the shyest and most easily frightened man in the parish, and he did not at all like the work that had been given to him. With trembling hands he helped to lift the coffin onto the cart, covered it with a cloth, and clicked to the horse. The road to Weatherbury was long, and the day was growing late, and a cold mist was beginning to rise from the meadows.

Halfway home Joseph passed a friendly inn, with a bright fire shining through the window, and his courage, which had been low all afternoon, failed him altogether. He told himself that one drink would steady his nerves and do no harm, and he left the horse standing and went inside. It was a decision that he would be teased about for the rest of his life, and one that he would never quite live down in the malthouse.

Inside he found some old friends, who were delighted to see him and demanded the news, and one drink became two, and then three, and the hours slid quietly by. The cart stood in the yard under the stars with its sad burden, forgotten, while Joseph told stories at the fireside. By the time he remembered it, the night was far gone, and a thin cold rain had begun to fall upon the covered cart.

At last the memory struck him like a bucket of cold water, and Joseph stumbled out to the yard, climbed onto the cart and drove off toward Weatherbury as fast as the tired horse could go. The lamps of the village were long out when he arrived, and the churchyard lay black and silent. He knocked, with a shaking hand, at the door of the farm, and waited miserably for someone to come and ask him what he had done.

The cart came into the farmyard long after midnight, and the coffin was carried into the house, where it was left for the night in the quiet of the hall. Troy was away from home on one of his errands, the servants had gone to bed, and only Gabriel and a few others were there to hear Joseph's miserable explanation. Nobody had the heart to scold him, for he looked so wretched that even the horse seemed sorry for him.

By the light of a lantern Gabriel read the words that had been chalked on the lid, which said Fanny Robin and child, and he understood in a moment what the poor girl's secret had been. Knowing how the village would talk, and how much pain it might cause his mistress, he took out his handkerchief and quietly rubbed away the last two words. It was a kind act, and, as it turned out, a useless one, for the whole truth was already on its way to the house.

That same night a rumour reached Bathsheba, passed from servant to servant in whispers, that Fanny had died with a child, and that Troy had been the father of it. She told herself that it could not be true, yet she could neither sleep nor rest, and the thought gnawed at her like a rat in the wall. The coffin lay below in the hall, and the truth, whatever it might be, lay inside it, waiting for anyone with the courage to look.

At last she took a candle and went softly down the dark stairs, in her nightdress and shawl, and stood beside the coffin in the silent hall. For a long time she did not move, for she knew that what she was about to do could never be undone, and that no wife should ever have to do it. The candle flame trembled in her hand, and the shadows leaped and fell on the old oak panelling of the hall.

At last she lifted the lid, and in the candlelight she saw Fanny's pale and peaceful face, with the infant lying still against her. Bathsheba stood for a moment quite unable to breathe, and then, as the whole truth rushed over her, she put her hand against the wall to keep from falling. The face of the sleeping girl was gentler than any reproach could have been, and that made the sight a thousand times harder to bear.

In that moment Bathsheba understood everything: the long silences, the sudden journeys, the careless tenderness, and the secret that her husband had carried into her house. It was Troy's child who lay there, and Troy's neglected love, and she herself had been only the second. The ground seemed to open beneath her, and she stood there cold and silent, too stunned even to weep for what she had lost.

While she stood there, the door opened, and Troy came in, still in his coat and smelling of the night air, with a careless word ready on his lips. The word died when he saw the open coffin and the white face of his wife. He walked slowly forward and looked down, and all the colour left his own face.

Troy knelt beside the coffin, bent over the dead girl and kissed her cold lips, while Bathsheba watched in horror. He told his wife, in a voice that was low and unsteady and utterly without pity, that this poor creature meant more to him, dead as she was, than Bathsheba had ever meant or ever could. Then he rose, walked out of the house, and left the door swinging on its hinges.

Bathsheba was left alone with the coffin and the dying candle, and the great silence of the house closed in around her. She sank down upon the stairs and wept, not for her pride, which was hurt, nor for her love, which was broken, but for the pale girl who had lain in the dark so long. Toward morning, worn out by grief and the long night, she slept at last where she sat.

The next day Fanny and her baby were laid in the churchyard at Weatherbury, in a corner beneath an old yew, with only a few mourners standing in the grey light. Gabriel was among them, and Bathsheba stood at the back with her face hidden by a veil, and Troy was nowhere to be seen. The vicar's voice carried softly over the wet grass and the old grey stones, and then the earth was filled in, and the small gathering went slowly home.

Troy rode into Casterbridge, and with the money that he could scrape together he paid for a fine headstone for Fanny's grave, cut with her name and a few tender words. He had never before spent a shilling on anyone but himself, and it surprised him to find how little the cost troubled him. It was the first generous thing that he had done in years, and he did it without telling a living soul.

Troy brought the stone to the churchyard, set it at the head of the grave and spent the whole of the afternoon planting flowers over the mound, kneeling in the soil with his coat off. He worked with a care that nobody had ever seen in him before, and by evening the grave looked like a small garden. For once in his life he was doing something that had no gain in it.

That night the rain came down in torrents, and the water ran from the church roof along the gutters and out through the open mouth of a stone gargoyle that leaned over the grave. It poured down upon the new mound as from a tap, and by morning it had washed the soil away like a spade. The little garden that Troy had made was torn up and scattered over the path, and the grave lay bare and sodden in the grey light.

In the morning Troy found his flowers lying in the mud, their roots in the air and their petals torn, and he stood for a long while looking at them in silence. All his careless pride seemed to run out of him, and he felt that even the sky had judged him and found him guilty. He turned and walked away from the grave without a word, and he did not go home.

He walked on across the country, through the heat of the day and into the long light of evening, until at last he came to the sea. Lulworth Cove lay below him, a small round bay of green water under white cliffs, and the sound of the waves filled his tired mind with a strange peace. He stood there on the shingle for a long time, doing nothing at all, while the colour slowly drained from the sky above the cliffs.

On a sudden impulse Troy undressed, left his clothes in a neat heap on the shore, and waded into the sea, where he began to swim with long, powerful strokes. He had not reckoned on the current that swept round the headland and drew everything outward, and in a few minutes he was far beyond the shelter of the cove. A small dark head, and then only the waves, were all that anyone could have seen.

A little later a passing boatman found the heap of clothes upon the shingle, and, seeing no one near, drew the natural and terrible conclusion. The news was carried back to Weatherbury, passing from mouth to mouth and growing sadder at every telling, until it came to the door of the farmhouse. By nightfall everyone in the village believed that Sergeant Troy had been drowned, and not a single person was sure how to feel about it.

Bathsheba, who had been struck dumb by the news, put on a black dress and sat alone at her window for hours at a time. She grieved for the husband whom she had loved, and, if she was honest, for the husband whom she had imagined, and she spoke to almost nobody. The farm went on around her as it always had, but she saw very little of it, and she did not ask for the news.

While Bathsheba grieved, Gabriel quietly kept the whole farm running, looking to the sheep, the barns, the harvest and the accounts, and asking nothing in return. He had never made a speech about it, and he never would, but day by day the work passed into his hands, as water finds its own level. The workers began to say that he was the real master of the place.

At last Bathsheba asked Gabriel to take the post of bailiff and to manage the whole farm on her behalf, and she asked it with a humility that she would once have found impossible. Gabriel accepted, thanked her, and made no mention of the past, and under his steady care the troubled finances of Weatherbury slowly began to mend. It was, he reflected, a better place than he had ever dared to hope for.

Months passed, and the winter came, and Boldwood, who had never stopped loving her for a single day, came once more to Bathsheba's door. He was thinner and graver than before, and there was something in his eyes that made her afraid. He had not come to talk of the weather or the price of corn, and she knew it before he had spoken a single word.

Boldwood begged her, with a humility that was painful to watch, to promise that she would marry him at last, and he said that he was willing to wait six long years for the day. He did not ask her to love him, he said, only to give him something to hope for. It was the plea of a man who has no other hope left in the world.

Bathsheba did not love him, and she hesitated a long time, for she knew very well what it meant to promise her future to a man for whom she felt nothing. But she remembered the valentine, her own thoughtless joke, and all that had come of it, and the weight of guilt pressed upon her like a stone. She felt that she owed him something for all the pain that she had caused, and that she could not simply send him away.

At last, with her eyes on the ground, Bathsheba said that if Troy was not found within six years, she would consider herself free, and she would marry Boldwood. It was a promise given more out of pity than out of love, and she did not like the sound of it as it left her lips. Boldwood took her hand and held it as if it were made of glass.

Boldwood was happier than he had been in all his solitary life, and the happiness went to his head like wine. He resolved to give a great Christmas party for all his neighbours, the first that his house had seen in years, and he sent a special invitation to Bathsheba. He fancied that on that night she would declare herself before all his friends, and the dream made him almost young again.

By Christmas Eve Boldwood's great house was glowing from cellar to roof, with candles in every window, garlands of holly on every door and fires roaring in every room. Long tables were loaded with meat, cakes and puddings, and the musicians tuned their fiddles in the hall. It had never looked so cheerful, and it had never, in all its long history, been so close to an evil hour.

Bathsheba had no wish to go, for she was still in mourning and she was uneasy in her mind, but Liddy argued, and a promise is a promise, and so she went. She arrived late, in a plain dress, and Boldwood met her at the door with an expression so full of joy that she could hardly meet his eyes. All the guests turned to look at her as she came in, and she felt each look as a small, sharp weight upon her.

In a quiet corner of the room Boldwood took her hands and begged her to promise once more that she would be his wife, and he pressed a ring into her palm as a pledge. Bathsheba was so confused and so sorry for him that she could not bring herself to refuse the gift, though she would not say the words he wanted. She slipped the ring into her pocket, feeling like a thief who has been given a treasure that she had never wished to hold.

Suddenly the great door swung open, and a gust of the winter night blew through the warm room and made the candles flicker. In the doorway stood a tall man in a long coat, with the collar turned up and a hat pulled low over his face, and the music faltered and died. One by one the dancers stopped, the laughter died away, and the whole company turned to stare at the stranger in the doorway.

The stranger stepped forward, removed his hat, and smiled, and a gasp ran round the room, for it was Sergeant Troy, whom everyone had believed to be dead for months. He looked straight at his wife, ignored the stunned guests and said in a cool, easy voice that she was to come home with him at once. Bathsheba's face went as white as the cloth on the table, and she gripped the back of a chair as though the floor had tilted.

Troy strode across the floor, took Bathsheba by the arm as if she had been a parcel and told her again that she was coming home. She shrank from him with a cry of fear, and the whole room fell silent, so that every guest could hear the clock ticking in the hall. Across the room, Boldwood stood quite still, and his face had turned to stone, and his eyes never left the soldier's hand upon her arm.

Without a word Boldwood crossed the room to the place where a gun hung on the wall, took it down and held it in his hands as a man might hold a Bible. His face was white and fixed, his hands did not shake, and the eyes of the guests followed him like those of people in a dream. Nobody moved to stop him, because nobody understood in time what he meant to do, and then it was too late for anyone to move.

Boldwood raised the gun and fired, and the sound of it filled the house like a clap of thunder, and Troy fell to the floor and lay still. A woman screamed, a chair crashed over, and then all the room was silent again except for the weeping of the frightened guests. It had happened in a moment, and it could never be undone, and every person in the room knew it as they stood there.

Boldwood laid the gun quietly on the table, as though he were putting away a tool after a day's work, and walked out of the house into the frozen night. He said not a word to anyone, and not one of the guests dared to stop him or to follow. The door closed behind him on the horror and the candlelight, and the cold wind from the hills blew through the empty hall.

Boldwood walked all the long cold miles to Casterbridge beneath the stars, along a road white with frost and silent as the grave, and he did not once look back. At the door of the county jail he told the astonished keeper that he had killed a man and that he had come to give himself up. They took him in and locked the door behind him, and in the morning the whole county knew that Farmer Boldwood was in a cell.

At the next assizes Boldwood was tried in the court at Casterbridge, in a long room that was crowded to the doors with people who had known him for years. They could hardly believe that this grave, courteous farmer, whom everyone had trusted, could stand in the dock on a charge of murder. He listened to the proceedings with an air of strange calm, as though they concerned somebody else.

Witness after witness told the court that Boldwood had always been the most honest and kindly of men, and several declared that his mind had been strangely clouded for a long time before that night. The tale of the valentine, the long pursuit and the promise given at the party was told, and listeners shook their heads at the sad confusion of it. Nobody in the room could honestly say that he had been himself in those last months, and many wept as they listened.

The jury found him guilty, and the judge, with a heavy face, spoke the sentence that the law required, that he must be put to death. A murmur ran through the crowded room, and then it fell silent, and Boldwood bowed his head with the calm of a man who has no more to lose. He asked for nothing, he said nothing, and he was led quietly away between two guards, with his head still bent.

But the people of the district could not forget his long years of honest living, and many of them signed a petition begging that his life should be spared, since it was plain that his mind had been unhinged. Gabriel was among the first to put his name to it, and the paper was sent to the proper authorities. The whole parish waited anxiously for a reply, and for many weeks nobody in the village could speak of anything else.

At last the reply came, and the sentence was changed: Boldwood was not to die but to be kept in prison instead, a punishment that was perhaps harder than death for so proud and gentle a man. Bathsheba heard the news with a mixture of relief and sorrow that she could not have put into words. She remembered the red seal and the hymn-book and the foolish laughter of that winter evening, and she wept bitterly.

After the trial Bathsheba shut herself away in the farmhouse, pale, silent and unwilling to see anyone, as if the whole world had become a place of sorrow. She had lost a husband whom she had once adored, and a man who had loved her in his own wild way, and she blamed herself for both. The curtains stayed drawn, and the fire burned unwatched in the grate, and the days went by without anyone to count them.

Gabriel went on running the farm, and every morning at the gate and every evening in the malthouse the villagers asked him how their mistress did. He answered kindly and truthfully that she was well in body and heavy at heart, and that time would do what no doctor could. He did not tell them how much he longed to comfort her himself, nor how little he believed that she would ever ask it of him.

Then, one evening, Gabriel announced that he meant to leave Weatherbury at the end of the year and try his fortune in California, where, it was said, a man could make a new life for himself. He gave no reason, but those who knew him guessed it, for he had stayed near one woman for years, with nothing to hope for. It was the plan of a man who, having borne a long and patient devotion without reward, had at last resolved to put the sea between himself and his sorrow.

Liddy brought the news to her mistress, who stared at her for a long moment and then turned her face to the wall. Bathsheba had never imagined that Gabriel Oak could go, any more than she had imagined that the hills could go, and the thought was suddenly unbearable. For the first time in weeks she wept for something that she still had the power to save.

At dusk she put on her shawl, slipped out of the house without telling anyone, and walked across the fields to the little cottage where Gabriel lived. She stood outside the door for a long minute, hearing the faint notes of his flute from within and feeling very foolish and very afraid. Then, with a hand that trembled a little in the dusk, she lifted her knuckles to the old wooden door and knocked.

Gabriel opened the door and stood quite still in the lamplight, with the flute in his hand and astonishment in his honest face. Bathsheba asked him, in a small voice, why he had decided to leave the farm after so many years, and whether he had meant to go without a word. He said that he thought it was best, and he did not meet her eyes.

They talked then as they had never talked before, without pride and without pretence, sitting by the small fire in his cottage. Gabriel told her that he had loved her since the day on the hill, that he had never stopped, and that he could not stay near her and go on saying nothing. Bathsheba listened with her hands in her lap and tears running down her face.

Bathsheba told him quietly that there was no one in the world whom she trusted as she trusted him, and that she had been blind for a very long time. She did not ask him to speak again, but she did not tell him that he must not, and he understood her. Gabriel looked at her for a long moment, and then he said that he would stay, and that he would never speak of California again.

In the spring Gabriel and Bathsheba were married very quietly at the village church, with a few friends beside them and none of the show that Bathsheba had once admired. The proud girl who had once laughed at a steady heart had learned its worth, and Gabriel, who had loved her through ruin, fire, storm and sorrow, felt his long patience rewarded. Few weddings in the county were ever so plain, and none were ever so true.

That night the friends gathered outside the farmhouse and sang beneath the windows, as the custom of the country was, and the old songs rose up through the cold, clear air. The music carried far across the quiet fields, past the barn and the malthouse and the hill where the sheep were sleeping, and the stars seemed to listen. Inside the house, Gabriel and Bathsheba sat together, quietly happy, and the long story of their lives had found its ending at last.
